scenarios.title: The Spreadsheet CFO
scenarios.you: Sam from Spendly. You sell expense software, about $6 to $9 per user a month.
scenarios.goal: Book a meeting with Linda and her CEO.

options.text: Hi Linda, it's Sam with Spendly. I'll be brief: we help construction firms close their books faster. Can I have 30 seconds to see if it's even relevant?
options.why: Name, reason, and asking for a tiny slice of time. That lowers her guard.

options.text: Hi Linda, Sam from Spendly. Do you have a minute?
options.why: Polite, but it hands her an easy no and no reason to stay.

options.text: Hi Linda! How's your day going so far?
options.why: Small talk on a cold call signals "salesperson" and wastes her first five seconds.

options.text: Hi Linda, Spendly is the number one AI-powered expense platform, trusted by 5,000 companies, and I'd love to show you a demo.
options.reaction: I'm going to stop you there.
options.why: A pitch and a demo ask before she even knows why you called.

context: We already have a process for expenses. It works.

options.text: Makes sense. How long does month-end close take your team right now?
options.why: Acknowledge it, then ask a question that measures the pain instead of arguing.

options.text: Totally fair. A lot of our customers said the same thing before they switched.
options.why: Social proof is okay, but it's still pushing, and you learned nothing.

options.text: Spreadsheet processes break as you grow. Are you sure it works?
options.why: Challenging her directly makes her defend her process.

options.text: Okay, no worries, I'll send you some info.
options.why: Folding at the first objection. Every buyer says this.

context: Eight days. Mostly chasing receipts from the job sites. Our superintendents never send them in.

options.text: Eight days of chasing. What happens when the books close late?
options.reaction: The bank wants our financials by the 10th. We've been late twice this year.
options.why: Dig into the impact. The bank deadline is the real reason to change.

options.text: That's really common in construction. Our app lets supers snap receipts right on site.
options.why: Relevant, but you jumped to a feature before you understood the impact.

options.text: Honestly, eight days is pretty normal for your industry.
options.reaction: Then why are you calling me?
options.why: You just told her the problem isn't a problem.

options.text: So if I got you down to two days, you'd buy today, right?
options.why: A hard close on a cold call before you've earned anything.

context: Look, what does this even cost?

options.text: It depends on how many people submit expenses. Usually 6 to 9 dollars a user. How many people in the field would be on it?
options.why: Give a straight range, then ask a question that scopes it.

options.text: I'd rather show you the value before we talk price.
options.why: Dodging price feels shady, even when you mean well.

options.text: For you, I can do 40 percent off our list price.
options.reaction: You don't even know what we need yet.
options.why: A discount before she sees value tells her your price is fake.

options.text: Honestly, if you have to ask, it's probably not for you.
options.why: Condescending. Never make the buyer feel small.

context: Sixty people times nine bucks... that's real money. I'd need the CEO to approve it.

options.text: Understood. What would he need to see to say yes?
options.reaction: That it pays for itself. He hates new software.
options.why: Find out the decision maker's criteria instead of guessing.

options.text: No problem. Could you forward him my email?
options.why: Passive. You just handed control of the deal to a forwarded email.

options.text: Can't you approve it? It's only about six grand a year.
options.reaction: That's not how it works here.
options.why: Shrinking the price and pushing past her process.

options.text: Can I just call him directly?
options.why: Going around your champion burns the relationship.

options.text: Let's do 20 minutes Thursday at 2 with you and your CEO. I'll bring the math on your eight-day close and the bank deadline. Does that work?
options.why: A specific time, the right people, and an agenda built on HER pain.

options.text: Can we find some time next week to talk more?
options.why: Vague next steps turn into ghosting.

options.text: I'll send you a demo video and a few case studies.
options.why: Content isn't a next step. Nothing is on the calendar.

options.text: Great, I'll send the contract over today.
options.why: Way too early. She hasn't seen anything or talked to her CEO.

endings.win: Meeting booked with Linda and her CEO for Thursday at 2.
endings.lose: Linda's gone. She's not taking your next call.

scenarios.title: The For-Sale-By-Owner
scenarios.you: Taylor, a listing agent at Coastline Realty. Commission is about 2.5%.
scenarios.goal: Get a sit-down at Frank's house.

options.text: Hi Frank, Taylor with Coastline Realty. I saw your sign on Elm. I know you're selling it yourself and I respect that. Can I ask how it's going so far?
options.why: Respect his choice, then get curious. He relaxes because you're not attacking it.

options.text: Hi Frank, Taylor with Coastline Realty. Have you thought about working with an agent?
options.reaction: Nope. That's the whole point of the sign.
options.why: Straight to the ask. He's heard it ten times this week.

options.text: Hi Frank, most people who sell on their own end up listing with an agent anyway.
options.why: Telling him he'll fail makes him dig in.

options.text: Hi Frank! I have a buyer who'd love your house.
options.why: A fake buyer gets found out fast, and then you're done.

context: I'm not paying some agent thirty grand to put it on Zillow.

options.text: That's fair, thirty grand is real money. What would an agent have to do to be worth it to you?
options.reaction: Get me more than I'd get on my own, I guess.
options.why: Agree with the part that's true, then let him set the bar.

options.text: Totally get it. Studies show agents get about 10 percent more on average.
options.why: Stats without trust bounce right off.

options.text: We do a lot more than put it on Zillow.
options.why: Defensive. Now you're arguing about your job.

options.text: I could do one percent if you list with me today.
options.why: Cutting your fee instantly tells him it was never worth 2.5.

context: I've had two showings in three weeks. One guy just wanted to see the pool.

options.text: Two showings in three weeks. When do you need to be moved out?
options.reaction: We close on a house in Boise in 45 days. So... soon.
options.why: The timeline is what makes this urgent for HIM, not you.

options.text: Did you follow up with either of them?
options.reaction: The pool guy never called back.
options.why: Fine, but it doesn't uncover why this matters.

options.text: That's because you're not on the MLS.
options.why: Lecturing him about what he did wrong.

options.text: Honestly, your price is probably too high.
options.why: Judging a house you've never walked through.

context: Forty-five days. Yeah. My wife's a little stressed about it.

options.text: What happens if it isn't sold by then?
options.reaction: We'd be paying two mortgages. We really can't do that.
options.why: Let him say the consequence out loud. Now he owns the problem.

options.text: That's a tight window, but it's doable.
options.reaction: That's what I keep telling her.
options.why: Reassuring him takes away the reason to act.

options.text: Then you really need an agent.
options.reaction: Don't tell me what I need.
options.why: Telling beats asking only in your head.

options.text: If you list with me, I guarantee it sells in 30 days.
options.why: An overpromise he knows is fake.

context: Look, what would you even do differently?

options.text: Honestly, I'd want to walk through it before I tell you anything. Usually it's pricing off real comps, pro photos, and getting it in front of agents with buyers ready right now.
options.reaction: Hm. That's more than I've done.
options.why: Humble, specific, and it earns the visit.

options.text: We'd put it on the MLS, do professional photos, and hold open houses.
options.reaction: I could hire a photographer myself.
options.why: A generic list he can copy himself.

options.text: We use a proprietary 47-point marketing system.
options.why: Jargon instead of substance.

options.text: Everything. Your listing photos are pretty rough.
options.why: You just insulted his wife.

context: I'm still not sold on the commission.

options.text: That's fine, you don't have to decide today. Can I come by Saturday at 10 and show you a net sheet, what you'd walk away with both ways? If selling yourself nets you more, I'll tell you.
options.why: Low risk for him, a specific time, and honesty that builds trust.

options.text: Can I send you a market report and follow up next week?
options.why: Nothing scheduled. He'll ignore it.

options.text: Think about it: would you do your own dental work?
options.why: A cheesy analogy that feels like a sales script.

options.text: The commission isn't negotiable, but trust me, it's worth it.
options.why: "Trust me" and a wall. Game over.

endings.win: You're sitting at Frank's kitchen table Saturday at 10.
endings.ok: Frank says he'll call you if it doesn't sell. He won't.
endings.lose: Frank hung up. The sign stays in the yard.

scenarios.title: The "I Need to Think About It"
scenarios.you: Andre from Shieldline. Term life insurance, about $30 to $40 a month for her.
scenarios.goal: Book a follow-up with Tina (and whoever she needs) at a real time.

context: Hi, this is Tina. Oh, you're the insurance guy? Um, I guess I have a few minutes.

options.text: Thanks, Tina, I'll respect your time. You filled out a quote form last week. What made you start looking?
options.reaction: My sister passed last year and her kids had nothing. It scared me.
options.why: Asking WHY she's looking uncovers the real reason, and it's a big one.

options.text: Great! I can get you a quote in about five minutes.
options.why: Efficient, but you skipped the human part.

options.text: Perfect. Are you a smoker?
options.why: Straight into underwriting questions feels like a form, not a conversation.

options.text: Did you know 40 percent of families would struggle within six months of losing a parent?
options.why: Scare stats make people shut down.

context: I have two kids, 7 and 10. It's just me.

options.text: That's a lot on your shoulders. If something happened, who would take care of them?
options.reaction: My mom, probably. But she's on a fixed income.
options.why: Now you know who the money is really for, and why.

options.text: Then coverage is really important for you.
options.why: True, but it tells her nothing new.

options.text: You'll want at least 500 thousand.
options.why: Prescribing before you understand her situation.

options.text: Don't worry, we'll get you covered today.
options.reaction: I don't want to rush into anything.
options.why: Rushing a cautious buyer makes her more cautious.

context: How much does something like this cost?

options.text: For a healthy 38-year-old, half a million for 20 years usually runs 30 to 40 a month. Does that range feel doable?
options.why: A straight answer and a check-in, so her real objection comes out.

options.text: It depends on your health, but I'll run the numbers.
options.why: Fine, but she wanted a straight answer.

options.text: Less than a coffee a day!
options.why: A cliché she's heard a hundred times.

options.text: Price shouldn't matter when it's your kids' future.
options.reaction: Well, it does matter. I have a budget.
options.why: Guilt instead of respect.

context: Money's tight. And honestly, I need to think about it.

options.text: Of course. Can I ask what part you'd be thinking about? The price, or something else?
options.reaction: ...I guess I'm scared I'll pick the wrong thing.
options.why: "Think about it" hides the real objection. You found it.

options.text: Totally understand. When would be a good time to follow up?
options.why: Polite, but the real objection stays hidden.

options.text: What's there to think about? Your kids need this.
options.why: Pressure plus guilt. She's pulling away.

options.text: Rates go up on your birthday, so waiting will cost you.
options.why: Fake urgency on a nervous buyer.

context: Like, what if I buy it and it's the wrong amount or the wrong kind?

options.text: That's a smart worry. Let's figure out the right amount together. What would your mom need each year to raise them?
options.reaction: Probably thirty thousand a year. Until they're 18.
options.why: Turn her fear into a simple math problem you solve together.

options.text: You can always change it later.
options.why: Reassuring, but vague.

options.text: Term is always the right kind, don't worry about it.
options.reaction: Okay, but how do I know?
options.why: "Don't worry" isn't an answer.

options.text: I'd actually recommend our whole life policy. It builds cash value.
options.why: Upselling a tight-budget buyer into the wrong product.

context: Okay, this is helping. I still want to talk to my mom.

options.text: That's a great idea since she'd be the guardian. Want to do a quick call with both of you Thursday around 7? I'll bring two options and you pick.
options.reaction: Yeah. Thursday at 7. She'd like that.
options.why: Invite the decision helper in, set a time, and make it easy.

options.text: Sounds good. Call me after you talk to her.
options.why: She won't. Nothing is scheduled.

options.text: Can't you just decide today? It's pretty simple.
options.reaction: I said I want to talk to her.
options.why: Ignoring what she just told you.

options.text: If you apply today, I can lock in this rate.
options.reaction: I think I'm going to go.
options.why: Pressure at the finish line.

endings.win: Thursday at 7 with Tina and her mom. She thanked you.
endings.ok: She said she'll call after she talks to her mom.
endings.lose: Tina stopped answering. The kids still aren't covered.

scenarios.title: The Price Shopper
scenarios.you: Mike at Harbor Toyota. A 2022 Camry SE, 28,000 miles, listed at $27,900 out the door.
scenarios.goal: Get Denise in today with the car ready.

context: Hi, I'm calling about the 2022 Camry on your site. What's the out-the-door price?

options.text: Happy to help. Is it the silver SE with 28,000 miles? I want to make sure I give you the right number.
options.why: Confirm the exact car first. It shows you're careful, and it buys you a question.

options.text: Out the door it's about 27,900 with tax and fees.
options.why: A straight answer, but you gave up your only leverage right away.

options.text: Great car! When can you come in?
options.why: Ignoring her question.

options.text: We don't give prices over the phone.
options.reaction: Then I'll call someone who does.
options.why: A 1998 policy. She's gone.

context: Yeah, that one. I've got a quote from another dealer at 26,500.

options.text: Nice, sounds like you've done your homework. Is theirs the same trim and mileage?
options.reaction: Um... I think theirs has 41,000 miles.
options.why: Compare apples to apples without bashing anyone.

options.text: We might be able to get closer to that.
options.why: Negotiating against yourself.

options.text: Their cars are probably auction cars with problems.
options.why: Trashing the other dealer makes you look desperate.

options.text: I'll beat it. 26,000, done.
options.why: Now she thinks every number you say is fake.

context: I don't really care about the miles. I just need something reliable. My commute is 80 miles a day.

options.text: Eighty a day, so about 20,000 miles a year. How long are you hoping to keep this one?
options.reaction: Forever. My last car died at 150k and it was a nightmare.
options.why: Her commute makes the mileage matter. Let her get there herself.

options.text: Then the Camry's perfect. It's super reliable.
options.why: True, but generic.

options.text: With 80 miles a day, the miles actually matter a lot.
options.reaction: I said I don't care about that.
options.why: Correcting her directly makes her defend it.

options.text: Have you thought about a hybrid? We have a Prius for 31k.
options.reaction: I'm trying to spend less, not more.
options.why: Upsell before you've earned the right.

context: So what's your best price? I need to decide today.

options.text: Fair. Before I give you a number: if the price works, is there anything else that would stop you from buying today?
options.why: Flush out the hidden objection before you spend your discount.

options.text: Let me talk to my manager and call you back.
options.reaction: I don't have time for games.
options.why: The classic manager dance. Buyers hate it.

options.text: I can do 26,800. That's my best.
options.why: Your "best" still lost.

options.text: Our price is our price.
options.why: A wall with no reason behind it.

context: They offered me 4,000 for my trade. It's a 2012 Corolla.

options.text: Tell me about the Corolla, the miles and condition? I'll have our appraiser give you a real number, no games.
options.why: Honest process. And now you both know 4,000 was generous.

options.text: We usually give more than other dealers on trades.
options.why: A vague promise.

options.text: 4,000 is generous for a 2012.
options.why: True, but it makes you the bad guy.

options.text: Forget the trade. Sell it on Craigslist.
options.reaction: I don't have time for that.
options.why: You just created more work for her.

context: Okay. So can you make this work or not?

options.text: I think so. Can you come in at 5:30? I'll have the car pulled up front, the appraiser ready, and the numbers written down, so it takes 45 minutes, not four hours.
options.why: A specific time, and you solved her real fear: wasting her evening.

options.text: Come by whenever and ask for me.
options.why: "Whenever" means never.

options.text: I'll need your credit application first.
options.reaction: I haven't even seen the car.
options.why: Paperwork before trust.

options.text: If I get it to 26,400, will you buy it right now over the phone?
options.why: Price-dropping and pressuring at the same time.

endings.win: Denise is on the lot at 5:30. The car is pulled up front.
endings.lose: Denise bought the other car with 41,000 miles.

scenarios.title: The Burned Homeowner
scenarios.you: Chris from SunPeak, knocking doors. $0 down, and options without a 25-year loan.
scenarios.goal: Get a real appointment when both homeowners are home.

options.text: Hi, I'm Chris with SunPeak. I'm doing quick energy checks on your street today. Are you the homeowner?
options.reaction: Yeah. We're not interested in solar.
options.why: Who you are and why you're there, in one breath.

options.text: Hi! Are you the homeowner?
options.why: A question before you've said who you are. Suspicious at a door.

options.text: Hi! Do you like saving money?
options.why: A cheesy line she's heard before.

options.text: Hi, I'm with the utility company, doing an inspection.
options.reaction: You're not with the utility. Bye.
options.why: Lying about who you are. The door closes.

context: We're not interested in solar. My neighbor got burned.

options.text: I'm sorry to hear that. What happened with your neighbor?
options.reaction: His bill went UP and he's stuck in a 25-year loan.
options.why: Let her tell the story. That's her real objection.

options.text: We're different from most solar companies.
options.why: Every rep says it.

options.text: That's exactly why you should go with a company like us.
options.why: Using her pain as your pitch.

options.text: Your neighbor probably didn't read the contract.
options.why: Blaming her friend.

context: His bill went up and he's stuck in a 25-year loan. So, no.

options.text: That's awful, and honestly, it happens. If you ever did look at it again, what would need to be different?
options.reaction: No loan. No surprises. And I'd want to see the real math.
options.why: Agree it happens, then let her write her own conditions.

options.text: We don't do 25-year loans.
options.reaction: Okay, so what do you do?
options.why: Good info, but it skips her feelings.

options.text: His system was probably too small.
options.reaction: You don't know anything about his system.
options.why: Guessing and being wrong.

options.text: Prices are going up next month, so now is the time.
options.why: Fake urgency on the most skeptical person on the street.

context: And what's our electric bill got to do with you anyway?

options.text: Fair question. What's it running in the summer?
options.reaction: Almost 400. My husband works nights and sleeps with the AC on all day.
options.why: Short answer, then a question. She keeps talking.

options.text: Most people on this street are paying 300-plus in summer.
options.why: About them, not her.

options.text: Solar can eliminate your bill completely.
options.reaction: That's what they told my neighbor.
options.why: The exact line that burned her neighbor.

options.text: I can get you $0 bills forever.
options.why: An overpromise that confirms her fears.

options.text: Four hundred with the AC running all day. What would you do with that money if most of it went away?
options.why: Make it personal. The money has a purpose now.

options.text: That's really high. We can probably cut it in half.
options.why: "Probably" is a weak promise.

options.text: Then you're throwing away almost 5 grand a year.
options.reaction: Don't tell me I'm throwing money away.
options.why: Right math, wrong tone.

options.text: Great, let me grab your electric bill and we'll start the paperwork.
options.why: Way too fast.

options.text: You shouldn't. Can I come back Thursday at 6:30 when your husband's up, and show you both the real numbers from your bill, no loans, no pressure?
options.why: Agree with her, include the husband, and promise what she asked for: real math.

options.text: No problem. Can I leave a flyer?
options.why: Polite exit, no appointment.

options.text: The tax credit might go away soon.
options.why: Pressure after she set a boundary.

options.text: What would it take to get you to sign today?
options.why: She just said no. You didn't listen.

endings.win: Thursday at 6:30 with Brenda and her husband. She said, "You're different."
endings.ok: She took a flyer. It's in the recycling.
endings.lose: The door closed. She's warning the neighbors about you.
